Prompted by a conversation with a programmer who resists AI coding tools, Salvatore Sanfilippo reflects on why he adopted them so quickly despite decades of valuing carefully handwritten code. He arrives at a mixed practice: use AI to realize larger product and systems ideas, while preserving manual programming as a focused medium for invention, learning, and craft.

## Key Ideas

- Sanfilippo contrasts his long-standing concern for code quality and robustness with a recent reversal: after roughly three decades of programming, he now uses AI to write most of his code. [00:03:09]
- He expects handwritten programming to persist in a role analogous to poetry: small, elegant, or genuinely novel programs can express ideas that influence much larger systems without requiring people to implement millions of lines themselves. [00:04:10]-[00:05:14]
- A new programming idea could also be expressed through an AI-built compiler and then demonstrated with small handwritten programs, separating implementation scale from the human contribution of a new form or concept. [00:05:14]
- His rationale for automating implementation is that project and product intuition remain central human contributions, while finite time and energy make implementation work a candidate for delegation. [00:06:18]
- Sanfilippo still sees value in several modes: fully AI-built projects governed through design decisions, AI-assisted code that receives line-by-line review, and entirely manual small programs. He weighs better structure against the practical difference between a week of work and a year. [00:07:18]-[00:08:24]
- A recent inference-kernel project strengthened his view because he reports that the AI-assisted implementation was faster and more stable than a handwritten alternative. More broadly, he values being able to realize and examine more of his ideas. [00:08:24]-[00:09:29]
- He wants small manual programs for aesthetics and learning to become a central part of his future practice rather than an occasional side activity, while acknowledging uncertainty about how that practice changes later in his career. [00:09:29]-[00:10:34]

## Practical Implications

- Choose among full delegation, close AI collaboration, and manual implementation according to the purpose of the project rather than enforcing one universal workflow.
- Preserve small experimental programs as a low-cost way to communicate new abstractions and test programming ideas.
- Compare implementation quality against delivery time, behavior, and the opportunity to explore more product ideas—not code aesthetics alone.
- Use tests and direct performance or stability measurements to challenge assumptions about whether handwritten or generated code is better.

## Questions and Tensions

- The claim that product and design intuition remain human domains describes the author's current experience, not a guaranteed long-term boundary.
- One inference-kernel comparison cannot establish that AI-generated implementations generally outperform handwritten ones.
- The artistic analogy leaves open how large AI-built systems should be maintained, audited, secured, and understood when small demonstrations are not enough.
- A mixed practice preserves manual craft, but the transcript does not define how developers should allocate time among its three modes.
